transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... I mean, I came in because things have just been really different lately. Ever since my sister and her new baby moved back into the house, it’s just been... a lot. You know? Like, I love them, obviously, but the house is so small and there's just stuff everywhere now, baby bottles and toys, and the crying—man, the crying just gets under my skin in a way I didn't expect. I’ve been way more on edge and, I don't know, just down than usual. I find myself snapping over the littlest things at the house, like if someone leaves a dish in the sink or the TV is a little too loud. And then, because I'm so wound up at home, I end up showing up to my classes at the community college or to my shift at the machine shop already completely drained. Like, I haven't even started the day and I'm exhausted. I’m still getting by, mostly, but I’ve definitely missed a couple of deadlines for my coursework, which isn't like me. And I even had to back out of helping build the set for the local theater production, which I usually love doing, because I just couldn’t keep everything straight in my head. It's just like my brain is too full of all the stress from home to focus on anything else, you know?
Have you been feeling anxious or worried about things beyond just the stress at home?

I mean... not really? Like, I wouldn't say I'm just sitting around worrying about random things, if that's what you mean. It really all just comes back to the house. 

Like, before my sister moved in, I was totally fine. I had my routine, you know? I'd wake up, get some coffee, maybe look over my notes for my classes, head over to the machine shop for my shift... everything was just normal and chill. I didn't stress about work or school because I had the energy to handle it. I knew what I was doing. But now, it's just... it's like the house is this giant weight. So I'm not anxious about, like, getting struck by lightning or the state of the economy or even my job itself. It's just that my job and my classes are so much harder to deal with *because* I'm already so drained from the house. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to read this chapter for my intro class, and all I could hear was the squeaky wheel of that baby walker going back and forth, back and forth on the kitchen linoleum, and my sister talking loudly on speakerphone about her baby daddy drama, and I just couldn't even process the words on the page. I just felt my chest getting tight because I couldn't escape the noise. I ended up just staring at the wall for twenty minutes. So the worry isn't really about other stuff out in the world, it's just... it's all tied to that house and how I can't get a single moment of peace to just think anymore. Everything else is only a problem because the house is a problem, if that makes sense.
Have you been feeling sad most of the day, nearly every day, since your sister moved back in?

No, no, I wouldn't say I'm sad like that. Not like, sitting around crying all day or feeling completely hopeless or anything. It's not this deep, dark depression where I can't get out of bed. It's more just... I'm incredibly frustrated, you know? And yeah, maybe a little down because I miss how things used to be, but it's not a constant, all-day sadness. 

Like, yesterday, for example, I actually had a pretty good morning. I left the house early, before anyone else was awake, and went to this little diner near the community college to grab breakfast. It was quiet, the coffee was good, and I actually felt totally fine. I was looking over some schematics for work and just enjoying the peace. But then, as soon as my shift ended and I realized I had to go back home, that's when my mood just completely tanked. I started dreading walking through the front door, knowing the baby would probably be screaming or my sister would be complaining about something. 

So it's not like I'm sad every single minute of the day. If I'm at the shop and I'm really focused on fixing a piece of machinery, or if I'm hanging out with a buddy away from the house, I can actually laugh and feel normal. It's just that the minute I'm back in that environment, or even just thinking about having to go back, I get so irritable and drained. It's like a switch flips. But yeah, no, not sad all day every day. Just... overwhelmed by the situation, I guess. It's really just the environment that's dragging me down, not some sort of constant sadness.
Have you been avoiding certain activities or places because of how they might affect your stress or mood related to your home situation?

I mean, avoid things? No, not really. I guess I've been doing the opposite, actually. Like, I don't avoid places because of the stress—I try to find places to go *to* avoid the house. I definitely haven't stopped going to work or anything like that. If anything, I try to pick up an extra shift at the machine shop if I can, just to have a reason not to be at home. 

And, you know, I mentioned the theater thing earlier, but that wasn't really about avoiding it because it would make me stressed. It was just that my brain was so fried from the house that I literally couldn't focus on measuring the wood or reading the blueprints for the set. I just kept messing up the cuts because my head was pounding from the lack of sleep. So I had to step back from that, but it wasn't because the theater itself was stressing me out. 

But yeah, as far as avoiding stuff... no. I still go to the diner, I still go to the shop, I still try to go to my classes at the community college, even if I'm dragging myself there. I'll even just sit in my car in the parking lot of the grocery store sometimes for an extra twenty minutes after I get off work, just scrolling on my phone or listening to the radio, just to delay having to walk through that front door. So it's not that I'm avoiding the outside world. The outside world is great. It's the inside world—my house—that I'm trying to stay away from as much as humanly possible right now.
Are there any social activities or gatherings that you've stopped attending because of how you've been feeling since your sister moved back in?

I mean, social activities... like hanging out with people? No, I haven't really stopped seeing my friends or anything like that. Like I said, I'll take any excuse to get out of the house right now. If a buddy wants to grab a burger or just, I don't know, drive around, I am the first one in the car. I need that time away from the noise and the chaos. 

But, I mean, as far as other stuff goes... I guess it has affected some things I do. Like, I'm still going to my classes at the community college, and I haven't missed any shifts at the machine shop, because I need the money and I need to pass. But I will admit, I've definitely slipped up a bit. I turned in a couple of assignments late for my intro to psych class, which isn't like me at all. Usually, I'm super on top of my deadlines. I have this whole planner system I use, color-coded and everything. But lately, with the baby crying at all hours and my sister constantly needing something, I just sit down to do the work and my brain is totally empty. I'll read the same paragraph five times and still not know what it said. So yeah, a couple of things have been late because I just couldn't get them done on time with everything going on.

And then there's the community theater thing. I think I mentioned that earlier, right? Yeah, the set project. I had to completely drop out of that. Which really sucks, because I love doing it. I've been helping build the sets for their plays since I was in high school. It's usually this great creative outlet for me, getting to use my tools for something other than industrial machinery, you know? Building the backdrops, figuring out the structural support for the platforms... it's fun. We were working on this really cool multi-level set for a mystery play, and I was in charge of the main staircase. But I just... I couldn't keep up. I was going straight from my classes to my shift at the shop, and then trying to squeeze in hours at the theater, all while getting maybe four hours of broken sleep a night because of the situation at home. I was exhausted. I was making stupid mistakes, like measuring things wrong or cutting the wood too short, which is a huge waste of materials and money for a community theater on a tight budget. It just got to be too much. I couldn't juggle the classes, the job, the theater, and the stress of living in that house. Something had to give, so I had to tell the director I couldn't finish the project. It really bummed me out, but I just literally couldn't keep up with everything anymore.
Have you been feeling like you need to escape or get away from your emotions when you're at home?

Escape my emotions? Um... no, I wouldn't really say it's like that. I mean, I'm not trying to run away from my own head or, like, numb out what I'm feeling. If I'm pissed off because the baby woke me up at 3 AM again, I know I'm pissed off, and I'm fine with feeling that way because, I mean, who wouldn't be, right? It makes total sense. It's not like I have these big, scary, overwhelming emotions that I can't handle and feel like I have to run away from. 

Like I was saying before about sitting in my car at the grocery store or taking extra shifts at the machine shop... I'm not doing that to distract myself from my feelings. I'm doing it to get away from the actual, physical house. The noise, the chaos, my sister's stuff just scattered everywhere. It's the environment I want to escape, not myself. If you put me in a totally quiet, empty room right now, I wouldn't be trying to escape my thoughts or my emotions at all. I'd probably just sit there and enjoy the absolute silence, or, honestly, I'd probably just fall asleep since I'm running on fumes anyway. 

So, yeah, no, I don't feel like I need to get away from my emotions. My emotions are just normal frustration about a really annoying situation. I don't have a problem with what I'm feeling inside. It's just the house itself—and the people in it—that I'm trying to get a break from.
Are you having trouble completing tasks or daily activities because of your current situation at home?

Yeah, I think I actually kind of touched on this a little bit a few minutes ago when I was rambling, but... yeah, it's definitely bleeding into my daily stuff. 

Like I said, I'm still physically getting myself to class, and I'm definitely still clocking in for my shifts at the machine shop. I have to, right? The bills don't stop just because my sister decided to turn our house into a circus, and I really need to keep my grades up if I want to actually get my degree. So I'm showing up. But as far as actually *completing* things when I'm at home? That's where I'm hitting a massive wall. 

Those late assignments I mentioned earlier? That is so incredibly rare for me. I usually sit down at my desk, open my laptop, look at my color-coded planner, and just knock the work out. Boom, boom, boom. I like being efficient. But now? I sit down, and I can hear the baby wailing right through the drywall, or my sister is blasting the TV because she says she "needs background noise," and I just end up staring at the screen. I literally can't process the words in my textbook. So a reading response that should take me maybe forty-five minutes ends up taking me three hours, or I just give up and pass out on my bed because I'm so exhausted. Which is exactly why those couple of assignments ended up being turned in late. I just couldn't get my brain to cooperate.

And then, of course, the community theater thing. Having to drop that set project was... I mean, it was a huge bummer. I really, really didn't want to do that. I had this whole idea for how to reinforce the steps on that staircase so it wouldn't creak when the actors ran up and down it during the play, but I just couldn't keep up with everything. My brain was just too foggy from the lack of sleep and the constant stress at home. I was making those stupid measuring mistakes, and I realized I was just going to ruin their good lumber if I kept trying to force it. I literally just couldn't juggle the shop, the classes, and the build all at once on four hours of sleep. Something had to go. So, yeah... I'm getting the bare minimum done to survive, I guess, but anything extra, or anything that requires real, deep mental focus at home... it's just not happening the way it usually does.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain your relationships with friends or family members outside of your household due to your current living situation?

Maintain relationships? No, honestly, it's almost the exact opposite right now. Like I was kind of saying earlier about grabbing a burger or driving around... my friends are basically my lifeline at this point. 

Usually, I'm the kind of guy who's totally fine just chilling in my room after a long shift at the shop or after I finish my reading for my classes. I'd just put my headphones on, maybe play some video games, or mess around with some sketches for the theater sets—well, when I was still doing the theater stuff, anyway. I was never really the guy who had to be out doing something every single night. But now? Man, I am blowing up my friends' phones. 

Just the other night, my buddy Dave—he works at this auto body place down the street from where I do my machining—he texted me at like 9 PM asking if I wanted to go to this 24-hour diner on the edge of town. Normally, on a Tuesday, I'd say no way, I have an 8 AM class and I need to stick to my schedule. But my sister was in the living room trying to get the baby to sleep by walking him back and forth, back and forth, and the floorboards were squeaking, and the kid was just screaming his head off... I literally grabbed my jacket, didn't even tie my boots all the way, and practically ran out the door. We sat at that diner for like three hours just drinking terrible coffee and talking about, I don't know, transmission rebuilds and whatever else. I didn't even care that I was gonna be completely wrecked for class the next day. I just needed to be anywhere but there.

So, yeah, my friendships are probably stronger than ever right now because I'm just constantly looking for an excuse to hang out. If a buddy says, "Hey, want to come help me clean out my garage?" I'm like, "Yes, absolutely, I will be there in ten minutes." And as for family outside the house... I mean, it's just my mom and me usually, and now my sister. I have an uncle who lives a couple of states over, but we just text on holidays anyway, so that hasn't changed at all. But yeah, anyone who *doesn't* live in that house? I am definitely not having any trouble keeping up with them. If anything, they're probably getting a little sick of me wanting to hang out so much.
Are you feeling like your living situation is affecting your ability to enjoy things you normally like to do?

Enjoy things? Um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, the stuff I usually like to do, I still really like doing it. It's not like the house being a total disaster zone suddenly made me hate my hobbies or whatever. 

Like, I still love going to the shop. Actually, I probably enjoy the shop *more* now than I did before my sister moved in. Just the other day, my boss had me working on this massive industrial lathe—we were re-sleeving this huge pump housing for a chemical plant down the river—and I was just entirely in the zone. The smell of the cutting fluid, the sound of the metal shaving off... I loved every second of it. It was great. And my video games, too. If I can actually get an hour where the baby isn't screaming, I'll throw my headset on and play some games with my buddies online, and I still get super into it. I still laugh, I still have a good time. It's not like everything is gray and boring now. 

If anything, I appreciate the fun stuff way more because my time at home is just so stressful. Like when Dave and I were at that diner the other night, I was having a genuinely good time. I wasn't sitting there miserable or staring at the wall. I was just eating my greasy hash browns and loving the fact that I couldn't hear a baby crying or a TV blaring. So, no, the ability to enjoy things is definitely still there. One hundred percent. I just... I just have to actually get away from the house to do it, you know? 

Like, if I'm trying to watch a movie in my living room and there's baby bottles everywhere and my sister is arguing on the phone with her ex-boyfriend again, obviously I'm not going to enjoy the movie. But that's just because of the noise and the distraction, not because my brain forgot how to like movies. If you put me in an actual movie theater right now, I'd have a blast. I'd probably get a huge bucket of popcorn and just completely check out for two hours. So, yeah, I definitely still enjoy things. I just need the right environment to actually experience it right now, because my house is definitely not that environment.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Wait, isn't that kind of what we just... I mean, like I was just saying a second ago, no, not at all. The interest is totally still there. 

Take that community theater thing I was talking about earlier. I didn't drop that because I didn't care about it anymore or because I lost my passion for it. I was actually super invested in it. I had spent, like, three days during my lunch breaks at the shop drawing up these blueprints on graph paper, trying to figure out the load-bearing joints for that staircase so it wouldn't wobble during this big dance number the cast was doing. I was really pumped to actually put it together, because I love that kind of structural problem-solving. So the interest was absolutely there, like, 110 percent. It just came down to the fact that I physically couldn't do it safely while running on zero sleep. If you magically gave me my old quiet house back tomorrow, I'd be right back in that theater with my tool belt on in a heartbeat. 

And it's the exact same with everything else. I even just bought this new open-world game on sale a few days ago that I've been dying to play, but I literally just haven't had a single quiet hour to sit down and boot it up without my sister asking me to hold the baby while she warms up a bottle or whatever. So, yeah, no lost interest here. I still want to do all my normal stuff. I'm just totally starved for the peace and quiet to actually *do* the stuff I'm interested in, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite since your sister moved back in?

Appetite? No, not really. I mean, I'm eighteen and I work in a machine shop half the day and take classes the rest, so I'm pretty much always starving, to be honest. Like, my appetite hasn't dropped off at all. 

Just yesterday on my lunch break, I housed this massive Italian sub from the deli next to the shop—like, extra capicola, provolone, oil and vinegar, the works, plus a huge bag of jalapeño chips and one of those giant blue Gatorades. And I was still hungry enough to eat half of Dave's fries when we went to that diner the other night, on top of my own hash browns and eggs. So, yeah, no problems at all in the food department. 

I guess the only thing that's really changed is *where* I eat, or maybe just *what* we're eating at home, because my mom is usually way too exhausted from helping with the baby to cook the way she used to. We used to do, like, actual sit-down dinners, you know? She'd make meatloaf, or chicken and mashed potatoes, that kind of thing. Now it's a lot of frozen pizzas or me just grabbing a burger from the drive-thru on the way home from campus because nobody wants to turn the stove on or rattle pots and pans with a fussy infant in the house. Plus, the kitchen table is usually covered in formula tubs and burp cloths anyway. 

But as far as how much I'm actually eating or wanting to eat? Nah, that's completely the same. I still eat like a horse. I think if I stopped eating on top of not getting any sleep, I'd probably just pass out on the shop floor, and you definitely do not want to pass out anywhere near a running lathe, let me tell you. So yeah, I'm definitely still getting all my calories in, no matter how crazy the house gets.
Are you finding that your current situation at home is significantly interfering with your ability to function at work or in your daily life?

Interfering... well, I mean, I’m still going to class and going to work. It’s not like I’m just lying in bed all day refusing to participate in life. Honestly, leaving the house to go to the shop or campus is the best part of my day right now because it's my only escape from the chaos. So I am definitely still showing up to the mandatory stuff. 

But, yeah, I guess it is messing with things a bit, if I'm being completely honest. Like, school is getting tricky. I’m taking this intro to CAD class—computer-aided design—which usually I’m totally fine with, but I actually turned in a couple of assignments late recently. I just couldn’t focus on drafting the 3D models at home with my sister yelling and the baby screaming, and by the time things finally quieted down around midnight, I was just literally passing out at my desk. My professor was pretty cool about it and only gave me a small point deduction, but still, I hate turning stuff in late. That’s really not like me at all. I usually have my stuff printed and ready to go a day early.

And then there's the stuff outside of work and school. Like I mentioned a few minutes ago with that community theater thing... I actually had to drop that project entirely. Building that set was going to be my big fun project for the month, and I'd already put in all that time on the blueprints, but I just realized there was absolutely no way I could keep up with everything. Trying to juggle the shop, my college classes, the insanity at my house, and then building a giant load-bearing wooden staircase? I just couldn't do it. I had to call the director and tell him I was out, which really sucked because they were counting on me, but I just didn't have the energy or the focus to do it safely. So, I guess, yeah, it is interfering, even though I’m still technically holding down my job and going to my lectures. I'm just kind of dropping the ball on the edges, you know?
Are you feeling like you're unable to fulfill your responsibilities or meet your expectations in your daily life because of how you've been feeling?

Yeah, I mean, I feel like we’re kind of touching on exactly what I was just talking about, you know? Like I just said with the CAD assignments and the theater set... that's pretty much exactly what's happening. I am still going to class and I'm still clocking in at work. I haven't completely dropped off the map or anything. I'm doing the mandatory stuff. 

But as far as my actual *expectations* for myself? Yeah, I'm definitely not meeting them, and it honestly really bothers me. Because, like I was saying, I’m usually the guy who has everything squared away. Turning in those CAD assignments late was a huge blow to my pride, even if the professor didn't make a massive deal out of it. Sitting there handing in something I knew wasn't my best work just because I couldn't keep my eyes open at my desk at home... it just sucks. I hate feeling like I'm slipping. 

And having to bail on the theater project? That really stung, man. Like I mentioned, I had all the blueprints drawn up on my lunch breaks, I had the load-bearing joints figured out, and I was so ready to get in there and build that staircase. I really pride myself on following through when I say I'm going to build something. But I just had to face facts that I couldn't keep up with everything. Trying to juggle the machine shop, my college classes, and a massive set construction project while living in a house that sounds like a literal daycare center 24/7... it was just impossible. Something had to give. So, yeah, I'm doing the bare minimum to get by and keep my job and my grades afloat, but I definitely feel like I'm failing to keep up with the standard I usually hold myself to.
Are you feeling like your current living situation is causing you significant distress or impairment in your ability to function socially or occupationally?

I mean, Doc, I feel like we’re kind of beating a dead horse here, because, yeah, it’s exactly what I’ve been saying for the last ten minutes. It's like you're asking the same thing but just using bigger words, you know? But yes, absolutely, it is causing me distress, and it's definitely impacting my social life and my school stuff. 

Like I was just explaining, I’m still going to class and I'm still clocking in at work at the machine shop. I'm not totally falling apart and hiding under my covers. I still get up, put my boots on, and go do my job because I need the paycheck for tuition, and honestly, the guys at the shop are great. But I’ve turned in a couple of assignments late for my CAD class now, which, again, is just so frustrating for me. I was literally sitting at my laptop the other night, trying to finish this 3D rendering, and my sister is just going off in the hallway about how nobody is helping her, the baby is wailing, the dog is barking because the baby is wailing, and I just couldn't think straight. I couldn't focus on the screen. So I ended up turning it in late, which is just... it's just really stressful for me to not be on top of my game like that. 

And then socially? Yeah, it's a huge hit. That's why I had to drop the community theater set project. I just couldn’t keep up with everything. And that really sucks because that wasn't just a construction gig for me, it was my main social outlet for the whole month. Usually, when we do those sets, it's a whole crew of us. We get in there, we measure out the lumber, we get the frames up, and then we order a bunch of pizzas and just hang out and talk while we paint or whatever. It's a really good time with good people. But I had to call the director and pull out completely because I just do not have the bandwidth. Between my shifts at the shop, trying to salvage my grades in my college classes, and dealing with the absolute circus my house has become... I just had nothing left in the tank for anything social. So, yeah, I'm doing the bare minimum of going to work and school, but anything beyond that—like my hobbies or hanging out with the theater crew—is just completely gone right now.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since your sister moved back in?

Sleep? I mean, not really? Like, my actual sleep is fine. It’s not like I’m lying in bed staring at the ceiling because my brain is spinning or anything like that. Honestly, once I actually get to close my eyes, I’m out like a light. I mean, you gotta figure, between working shifts at the machine shop—which is pretty physical, you know, moving heavy metal stock around, standing on concrete floors all day—and then dealing with my college classes, I’m usually completely wiped out by the end of the day. So the sleeping part isn't the issue. 

It's more just... getting to the point where I *can* sleep, if that makes sense. Like I was saying before about passing out at my desk, the house is just so loud now. My room is right next to the hallway, and it’s an older house, so the floorboards creak like crazy. When my sister is trying to get the baby down, she does this pacing thing back and forth, back and forth, right past my door. And the baby is fussing, and then the dog gets anxious because the baby is fussing, so his nails are clicking on the hardwood... it’s a whole production. It usually takes her like an hour just to get things settled down. 

So, yeah, I might be staying up a little later just waiting for the circus to pack up for the night so I can actually get some peace and quiet, but my actual ability to sleep? No, I wouldn't say that's changed. Once it's finally quiet and my head hits the pillow, I sleep like a rock. I'm just too exhausted not to.
Do you feel like your frustration and irritability are constantly with you, even when you're not directly dealing with the stressors at home?

I mean, no, not constantly. It's not like I'm just walking around angry at the world all day, you know? Like, when I'm at the machine shop, I'm actually pretty focused. It's loud in there, but it's a good kind of loud. You got the lathes running, the CNC machines going, guys yelling over the noise to coordinate on a job... it's organized chaos, and I know exactly how to operate in it. I like the smell of the cutting fluid, the feeling of the metal shavings under my boots. When I'm there, I'm just dialing in the tolerances on whatever piece I'm working on, and I'm not really thinking about my sister or the baby or the dog pacing the hallway. I'm just doing my job. 

And it's the same when I'm in class, for the most part. If I'm sitting in a lecture hall and the professor is going over, I don't know, fluid dynamics or whatever, I'm engaged in that. I'm taking my notes, I'm trying to wrap my head around the formulas. I'm not sitting there stewing in anger about my living situation. 

It really just hits me when I have to go back home, or when I'm trying to do something that requires me to be at home, like those CAD assignments I was telling you about. That's when the frustration really boils over. Like, I'll pull into the driveway, and I can already feel my jaw clenching before I even turn off the ignition, because I know what I'm walking into. I know there's going to be baby toys scattered all over the living room, and my sister is going to be stressed out and complaining, and the dog is going to be whining because he hasn't been walked. That's when I get irritable. But once I'm out of that environment, once I'm away from the actual source of the stress, I usually cool down pretty quick and get back to being my normal self. It's really just tied to the house and everything going on in it right now.
Do you find yourself short-tempered or snappish with others even when you're not at home or directly dealing with your sister or the baby?

No, no, definitely not. Like I was saying a minute ago about how I feel when I'm at the shop, I really try to keep all that house drama completely compartmentalized. I mean, you really can't afford to be snapping at people when you're working around heavy machinery anyway. If you're losing your temper or acting erratic while someone is trying to run a lathe or calibrate the mill, somebody is gonna end up losing a finger, you know? So I keep it totally professional. 

And honestly, the guys at work are great. Like, there's this older guy, Dave, who works the station right next to mine, and he's always busting my chops about being the young college kid of the crew. He'll make jokes about me needing a juice box or whatever, and I just laugh it off. I throw it right back at him. If I was actually walking around on a hair-trigger all day, I'd probably snap at him, right? Because he can be a lot sometimes. But it doesn't bother me at all. I just joke right back. 

And it's the same deal at school. I mostly keep to myself in lectures, but if I have to talk to a professor or do a group project, I'm totally normal. I'm not biting anyone's head off. I actually make a really conscious effort to leave the stress in my truck. Sometimes I'll literally just sit in the parking lot for like five minutes before I clock in for my shift, just staring at the steering wheel, taking a deep breath, and telling myself, okay, leave the sister stuff here, leave the baby crying here, just go be a mechanic. Because it's not Dave's fault my house is a disaster area right now, you know? It's not my professor's fault, either. So I definitely don't take it out on them. It's really just... it's just when I cross the threshold back into my own house that I get short with people, because that's where the actual problem is. Outside of that, I'm my regular self.
Are you finding it hard to do daily tasks because of how you're feeling?

Well, I mean, I’m still getting out of bed and doing the main things, you know? Like I was saying, I’m still going to work, still clocking in for all my shifts at the shop. I haven't missed a day there, because, frankly, I need the paycheck, and honestly, it’s my escape anyway. And I'm still physically showing up to all my classes. I'm sitting in the lecture hall, taking the notes. 

But... yeah, I guess the actual execution of some things is starting to slip, if I'm being completely honest. Like those CAD assignments I was telling you about earlier? I’ve actually turned in a couple of them late recently. Which really isn't like me at all. Usually, I’m super on top of my deadlines, but trying to focus on complex modeling when I'm just so mentally drained from the house situation... I just end up staring at the screen, listening to the floorboards creak and the baby cry, and I get absolutely nowhere. So I've missed a couple of cutoffs for those. 

And then, there was this other thing, too. I was actually volunteering to help build sets for the community theater downtown. It was supposed to be this really cool side project where I could use some of my shop skills—doing some carpentry, rigging up some structural metal frames for the backdrops, that kind of stuff. I was actually really looking forward to it, because it's a different kind of building than what I do at work. Traumatic? Uh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, unless you count, like, breaking my arm when I was ten because I fell off a dirt bike, but that’s just... that's just being a kid, you know? Honestly, my life before all this has been pretty, I don't know, boring? Like, standard issue.

Honestly, up until my sister and the baby moved back in and completely turned my house upside down, my day-to-day was just... wake up, go to class, go to the shop, come home, maybe play some video games or work on my truck, go to sleep. It was just a really steady, predictable routine. I liked it that way. I'm a guy who likes a routine, which is probably why I like machining so much. You follow the steps, you get the result. So, yeah, no trauma or anything like that in my past. Just... just the current headache with my house turning into a daycare center. Well, I mean, I definitely feel *better* when I'm out of the house, like I was saying. I can put on my work boots, joke around with the guys, and just be my regular self for a few hours. But... My sister and her newborn are still living with us right now. They're still in the house, still taking up all the space, the baby is still waking everybody up at all hours, and all those bouncy seats and bottles are still covering every inch of the kitchen counters. So even when I'm at the shop or sitting in a lecture, there's always this thought in the back of my head that I have to go back to it as soon as I clock out. It's like this lingering dread just waiting for me in my truck. 

So, yeah, I can compartmentalize and act normal while I'm running a machine or talking to my professor, but all of this exhaustion and being short-tempered when I walk through my front door... it's all still tied to that same change at home. It's not like the problem is solved and I'm just holding onto the stress for no reason. The stress is still actively happening because they are still living there. Until she actually gets her own place and I get my quiet house back, I feel like I'm just kind of... bracing myself, you know? Like I'm just surviving it day by day while the whole thing is still going on.

I mean, no, not constantly. It's not like I'm just walking around angry at the world all day, you know? Like, when I'm at the machine shop, I'm actually pretty focused.
